So what are multiranges and why should you care? Multiranges allow you to operate on sets of ranges in a single operation. This is particularly useful when working with large datasets that are divided into intervals, as it makes it possible to perform complex queries that would otherwise require multiple steps.

For example, imagine you have a data set that represents temperature readings for a week, with temperature values ranging from -10 to 40 degrees Celsius. If you want to find all the time intervals where the temperature was above 30 degrees, you could use a multirange to represent the range of values from 30 to 40, and then perform a query that checks whether each temperature reading falls within that range. The result would be a list of the time intervals where the temperature was above 30 degrees.

How routing algorithms work
When you want to visit a web site, your network card will look at the destination IP address and send the packet out to your default router which might forward it out further until it reaches a cache server, like Cloudflare.
When your default router forwards packets, it uses what's called a routing table. This table contains a list of all valid IP addresses it knows how to reach and how to reach them efficiently. More specifically, each "record" in the routing table holds a destination network address, a subnet mask indicating which bits of the destination IP address define the network, and the next hop IP address which tells the router where to send packets for that network. about how to reconcile quantum physics with Einstein's general theory of relativity.

Two black holes are quantum mechanically entangled like particles like photons. If we look at the two black holes individually, they'll be fully described by general relativity as vacuum regions with particular horizons. But once they're entangled, their states can no longer be described by separately looking at them. In general relativity, the black holes are black because they trap light and all information within their event horizons, but this picture breaks down once you have entanglement. In that case, some information might escape.

For quantum physics to be consistent with general relativity, the universe must have certain properties, including "firewalls"—intensely hot regions right around black hole horizons. Information entering a firewall would be effectively destroyed. Exposing the information to an external observer who is entangled with the black hole would then allow the transmission of signals faster than light, something that general relativity suggests shouldn't happen.

ipfs-deploy can be installed globally using npm or yarn. This makes it easy to run with the `ipfs-deploy` command.

```sh
npm install -g ipfs-deploy

This is because PostgreSQL relies heavily on indexes for efficiently query these range columns. In addition, ranges can be fragmented, as PostgreSQL can split a range by multiple ranges using different indexes, which inefficient when there is a lot of records in a column. PostgreSQL 14 solves this problem with the multirange.
Multiranges in simple terms, is a way to store multiple ranges in a single column, and in this same column, it reduces the complexity of having multiple ranges, using new compression techniques. This results in a significant reduction in the number of rows required and a simplification of query planning.
Benefits of multiranges in PostgreSQL:
    improved query performance: By reducing fragmentation and simplifying query planning, multiranges can significantly improve the performance of range-based queries.
    Space efficiency: Multiranges reduce the storage requirements of range data

Installation
To install ipfs-deploy globally, run:
`npm install -g ipfs-deploy`
After installation, you can run `ipfs-deploy --help` to see the available commands and options.
Usage
The basic usage of `ipfs-deploy` is to deploy a directory of static files to IPFS. The command will recursively add all files in the directory to IPFS, and then create a pinset containing the hash of the added files. This pinset can be used to easily replicate the same set of files on other IPFS nodes.
For example, to deploy the `./static` directory to IPFS:
`ipfs-deploy ./static`

The nodeacy.js is a tool included in Rome toolchain for analyzing dependencies graph using the Acyclic Graphs dependency detector ([Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.13477), [Demo](https://apis.shebang.dev/rome-dependency-analyzer/)). The tool is used to analyze the dependency graph for a given JavaScript project and identify any cyclic dependencies.

## Language(s)

JavaScript

## How it works

The `nodeacy.js` tool works by analyzing the dependency graph of a JavaScript project. It does this by parsing the source code of the project and identifying all the dependencies. It then uses the Acyclic Graphs algorithm to detect any cyclic dependencies in the graph. If cyclic dependencies are detected, the tool will report them to the user.

## Features

- Detects cyclic dependencies in the dependency graph of a JavaScript project.
- Provides a report of all detected cyclic dependencies.
- Custom tool, no third-party dependencies.

work with intervals of continuous values, providing a more intuitive way to store and query data within defined boundaries. The introduction of multiranges in PostgreSQL 14 significantly extends the flexibility of this feature, enabling developers to define ranges composed of multiple sub-ranges, each potentially with different attributes. This capability opens new avenues for data modeling, especially for applications that deal with complex intervals or time intervals spanning discontinuous periods. Introduction to Multiranges In PostgreSQL, a range represents a contiguous segment of a set of values, for example, a span of dates, numbers, or even arbitrary values like geometric objects. Traditionally, ranges are defined with fixed properties for start and end values. Multiranges, introduced in PostgreSQL 14, allow these properties to be repeated. This means that a multirange can cover multiple, potentially disconnected, or disjointed ranges of values within the same type. For example, a multirange of timestamps could represent a set of discontinuous time periods, such as the business hours for multiple days with different opening and closing times or periods when a service is unavailable.

A new type of robotic arm prosthesis uses a direct connection to the brain to provide a sense of touch without connecting to nerves and muscles. The 2009 study from a team of researchers in Switzerland hopes to improve significantly on previously available prosthetic arms. Unlike previous nerve interface technologies that required the attachment and stimulation of peripheral nerves, this technology bypasses the nerves entirely by connecting directly to the brain. Instead of inducing movements via signals delivered to nerves, this new technology provides sensory feedback directly to the brain where it is interpreted as the feeling of touch. This is accomplished using a variant of the Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) technology. In studies, patients using the new arm reported new awareness and enhanced ability to adapt movements to better interact with objects, beyond what had been observed using the traditional nerve interface approach. Using BaM, a single GPU can access and work on many GBs of data from an SSD without running into bottlenecks. Nvidia also claims that BaM makes it possible to train deep learning models using less VRAM. How is this possible? Ideally, a multi-bnode DGX Super system should be used to train deep learning models. This requires multiple GPUs to access the same data simultaneously. However, BaM allows you to run this workload on a DGX system with a single GPU by leveraging the NVLink interconnect. In a single GPU scenario, BaM would replicate the data being processed on the NVLink. Hence, the GPU would be capable of accessing the data mirrored on the NVLink. This feature also makes it easier to run inference without performance degradation when running it on a single GPU.

about 20% of the oceans had been mapped. Aasif Shakeel Malik is one of the researchers working towards this goal. He's with the University of Exeter in the UK. His work involves using a type of technology called LiDAR. "LiDAR stands for light detection and ranging," Malik told VOA. "Essentially we use it to send a laser beam down into the water. The beam gets scattered off the surface of the seabed, travels back up to the sensor on the ship, and measures the time taken for that pulse to return. Using that information, what we can do is estimate the distance to the seabed, from which we can then create a map of what the seabed looks like." But LiDAR has limitations. "It works relatively well in clear water conditions," Malik explained. "However, if there's cloudier conditions on the surface of the ocean or if there's more turbidity in the water, for instance, if there's more sediment in the water making it appear slightly murky, what happens is the light gets dispersed more across the ocean, essentially gets scattered, and this gives us a less accurate estimation of the depth of the water."

The modification was made using a standard technique that involves inserting a gene that acts like a light-sensitive sensor into the animal's genome. This sensor is derived from a special type of bacteria that reacts to different wavelengths of light. The researchers fused this sensor to a green or red fluorescent protein that glows when activated. They inserted this modified gene into jellyfish cells and watched what happened. These cells produce the sensor protein that then lights up when exposed to blue light, causing the cells to glow either green or red. This allowed the team to isolate specific cells and view how different areas of the animal's network respond to light stimulation. The sensor became part of that cell's genetic code, so it continued to glow when the animal's neurons fired. This meant the researchers could see which parts of the jellyfish were active without having to stimulate the animal. This is an advanced form of optogenetics that uses light to control brain cell activity.

Quantum entanglement is a peculiar phenomenon in which two or more objects become linked so that no matter how far apart they are, they remain correlated when one is measured. Physicists theorize that entanglement could be the key to transmitting information faster than light, potentially enabling instantaneous communication across vast distances. Entropy and information entropy are measures of randomness and disorder. At the quantum level, entropy is measured in units of bits. A bit is a binary unit of information that can have two possible values, 0 or 1. The more bits an object contains, the greater its uncertainty or randomness. At zero bits, there is no randomness, and the object has a definite state. For example, a coin has one bit of entropy. Before it is flipped, its state is uncertain: it can be either heads or tails (a 50-50 probability).

This research is ongoing but the findings are promising for the energy storage industry, as it addresses the current speed limitations of lithium-ion batteries. Using an innovative technique called nanophoresis, the scientists were able to inject microscopic bubbles filled with CaSR-RMS into the bloodstream while simultaneously irradiating the bubbles with sound waves.
